name: Functional MRI Interpretation
title: Functional MRI Interpretation
answer: Functional MRI interpretation uses AI to map brain activity from blood oxygen level dependent signals, turning four dimensional scans into maps of networks, task activation, and resting state connectivity. It supports neurosurgery planning, research into cognition and psychiatric conditions, and clinical review of language, motor, and memory areas. The work sits between radiology, neurology, and computational neuroscience, and it is distinct from structural MRI reading because the signal is indirect and noisy.

sections.body: Functional MRI interpretation uses AI to map brain activity from blood oxygen level dependent signals, turning four dimensional scans into maps of networks, task activation, and resting state connectivity. It supports neurosurgery planning, research into cognition and psychiatric conditions, and clinical review of language, motor, and memory areas. The work sits between radiology, neurology, and computational neuroscience, and it is distinct from structural MRI reading because the signal is indirect and noisy.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Models typically run on GPU servers or hospital imaging clusters, with preprocessing pipelines for motion correction, slice timing, and spatial normalization. Many tools use standard neuroimaging formats like NIfTI and BIDS, and inference can happen on a workstation for a single subject or on high performance computing for group studies. Cloud services are used for large cohorts, but clinical deployments often stay on premises because of patient data rules.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by training convolutional networks, transformers, or graph neural networks on labeled fMRI volumes, often after parcellating the brain into regions or projecting data onto a surface. Supervised models learn to classify tasks, detect language lateralization, or segment resting state networks, while self supervised and generative models learn representations from unlabeled scans. Human experts still review the output against structural images and clinical context, because fMRI activation is a statistical map, not a direct picture of neural firing.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on patient privacy, model bias across scanner types and populations, and the danger of overreading weak activation as a hard boundary for surgery. Provenance requires recording scanner field strength, acquisition parameters, preprocessing steps, and model version, because small changes can flip a result. Liability is unsettled when a model misses an eloquent area or produces a false activation, and regulatory clearance usually treats these tools as decision support rather than autonomous diagnosis.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward foundation models pretrained on large brain imaging archives, then adapted to small clinical datasets, and toward real time fMRI for presurgical mapping and neurofeedback. Multimodal models that combine fMRI with structural MRI, diffusion tractography, and EEG are likely to improve localization of function. The main open problems are generalization across sites, interpretability of attention maps, and validation against direct cortical stimulation, which remains the reference standard.
